title: One receipt becomes two item rows: flatten nested data deliberately
goal: Keep the flexible original payload while projecting predictable rows for analytics.
concept:
A paper receipt has one header and several item lines. JSON often uses the same shape: one order contains an items array. A semi-structured VARIANT keeps that nested shape. Flattening turns each array element into a correlated row.

Parse once, preserve the raw record, then project stable columns such as order_id, sku, and qty.
example:
Order R7 contains two items: two units of SKU A and one of SKU B. Switching to item rows repeats R7 while emitting two child rows. That repetition preserves the parent-child relationship.

A malformed payload is different from an empty array. Strict parsing stops it; tolerant parsing can quarantine it, but null must not silently mean “zero items.”

use_case.when: Use this when producers add optional fields or nested arrays faster than a rigid ingestion schema can evolve.
use_case.example: Land order JSON in a bronze table, retain the original VARIANT, then flatten items into a silver line-item table.
use_case.decision: Use VARIANT for genuine flexibility and typed columns for stable high-value fields. Flatten only needed paths because row counts can grow quickly.

practice: Predict the row count for R7. Switch between nested, flattened, and malformed states; explain what each preserves.
boundary: The browser uses one hand-authored receipt. It does not parse JSON, infer schema, run a distributed plan, or reproduce product errors.
js:
function variantPaint(){const v=jsonState.value==='valid',f=jsonView.value==='flat';if(!v)world.innerHTML='
Parse failed
Quarantine raw bytes; this is not zero items.
';else if(!f)world.innerHTML='
R7 · Ava
items=[A×2, B×1]

1 parent row; children remain nested.

';else world.innerHTML='
R7 · A · qty 2
R7 · B · qty 1

2 item rows; R7 repeats for correlation.

';}jsonState.onchange=variantPaint;jsonView.onchange=variantPaint;variantPaint();
questions: R7 has two objects in items. How many item rows should it emit?
Flatten counts array elements, not total quantity.
Tolerant parsing returns null. What is safe?
Treat it as a parse/NULL state requiring explicit handling
Parse failure and an empty array are distinct.
Why keep raw VARIANT after typed projection?
Controlled reprocessing and audit of unprojected fields
Raw data supports later projection but does not replace contracts.

steps.note: Emit one correlated row per item.

steps.code:
row_count=len(rows)
unit_count=sum(r["qty"] for r in rows)
steps.note: Count child rows separately from quantity.

walkthrough.limit: Executed local Python only; no vendor SQL ran.

visual_explanation: The visual changes one parent into two correlated children and keeps malformed input separate from an empty array.
written_questions: Which fields become typed silver columns first?
How will parse failures remain replayable?

product_sections.title: Databricks: parse VARIANT, then explode only items
product_sections.html:
Use case. Land changing order JSON without discarding new fields, then create an item-level silver projection.

Prepared real lab. Use an authorized non-production Databricks SQL warehouse or cluster and Unity Catalog schema. Use DBR 15.4 LTS or later for the documented VARIANT query path. The operator needs create/modify privileges and compute; selected compute incurs cost.

9-minute route. First minute: due product recall. Then predict R7 row counts, advance the SQL, and explain malformed-input handling.

The SQL is not run on Databricks. Buttons run a local JavaScript model.

CREATE TABLE study20.bronze_orders (raw VARIANT);INSERT INTO study20.bronze_orders SELECT parse_json('{"order_id":"R7","items":[{"sku":"A","qty":2},{"sku":"B","qty":1}]}');SELECT raw:order_id::STRING, item.value:sku::STRING, item.value:qty::INT FROM study20.bronze_orders, LATERAL variant_explode(raw:items) item;

Failure/fix. parse_json errors on malformed input; deliberately quarantine with raw bytes, optionally using try_parse_json. VARIANT has documented clustering and operation limits.

product_sections.html:
Use case. Keep a nested receipt in VARIANT and emit one relational row per item.

Prepared real lab. Use an authorized non-production Snowflake account, schema, and active warehouse. The role needs create/insert/select privileges; warehouse use costs credits.

9-minute route. First minute: due product recall. Then predict R7 rows, advance SQL, and distinguish null, empty array, and parse failure.

The SQL is not run on Snowflake. Buttons run a local JavaScript model.

title: A clock can move backward: measure elapsed time with a monotonic source
goal: Use a monotonic clock for durations and a wall clock for human timestamps.
concept:
A kitchen timer measures how long the cake baked. A wall clock tells when dinner started. Correcting the wall clock should not make the timer say “minus two seconds.”

A wall clock maps to calendar time and may jump. A monotonic clock moves in one direction and is intended for elapsed comparisons.
example:
A request starts at 12:00:00.000. During 250 ms of work, the wall clock is corrected backward by two seconds. Wall subtraction says −1750 ms; monotonic subtraction still says 250 ms.

long start = System.nanoTime();
work();
long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - start;

use_case.when: Use this for deadlines, retry backoff, cache-expiry checks, latency metrics, and local lease intervals.
use_case.example: A Java service enforces a 500 ms local deadline even if time synchronization adjusts the wall clock.
use_case.decision: Use wall time for audit timestamps. Use monotonic time for local duration; its origin is arbitrary and it is not comparable across machines or restarts.

practice: Toggle source and a backward correction. Predict the duration.
boundary: The browser uses fixed values; it omits clock resolution, scheduler pauses, VM suspension, and distributed uncertainty.
js:
function clockPaint(){const m=clockKind.value==='mono',b=clockCorrection.value==='back',e=m?250:(b?-1750:250);world.innerHTML='

'+(m?'Monotonic':'Wall-clock')+' subtraction: '+e+' ms.

'+(e<0?'Impossible duration: wrong clock.':'Meaningful duration in this model.')+'

';}clockKind.onchange=clockPaint;clockCorrection.onchange=clockPaint;clockPaint();
questions: Wall time jumps back 2000 ms during 250 ms of work. Result?
End wall time can be earlier than start.
nanoTime is documented for elapsed timing.
A calendar timestamp comparable across machines

steps.note: Wall time moves back while monotonic advances.

walkthrough.limit: Executed Java 17 arithmetic with synthetic readings; it did not alter the host clock.

visual_explanation: The correction arrow changes the wall timeline while monotonic elapsed time stays 250 ms.
written_questions: Name one elapsed-time and one calendar-time use.
Why can a persisted monotonic reading fail after restart?

title: Keep checkout, drop recommendations: design a tested degraded mode
goal: Preserve the critical customer path when an optional dependency is slow.
concept:
A restaurant can still serve dinner when the dessert printer breaks. If every meal waits for dessert, an optional feature became a critical dependency.

Graceful degradation keeps minimum useful service working while omitting optional work. Leaders must name the outcome that survives, acceptable quality loss, and evidence that the fallback was exercised.
example:
Checkout calls payment, inventory, and recommendations. Recommendations rise from 80 ms to 4 seconds. Payment stays green, but checkout p99 becomes 4.2 seconds.

Contain with a 150 ms recommendation budget and omit that panel. Orders continue. Then repair the recommender and verify the fallback did not hide pricing, inventory, or payment errors.

use_case.when: Use this when an optional dependency can consume a critical path’s latency or capacity budget.
use_case.example: Return checkout confirmation without personalized recommendations after 150 ms.
use_case.decision: Degrade only acceptable quality. Do not hide corrupt prices, authorization failures, or data loss; those need fail-closed or explicit error behavior.

practice: Make recommendations slow and toggle fallback. Observe useful checkout.
boundary: The deterministic toy uses 100 requests and omits queues, retries, cohorts, regional failures, and correctness hazards.
js:
function degradePaint(){const s=Number(recLatency.value)>150,o=fallbackMode.value==='on',n=s&&!o?0:100;world.innerHTML='

Useful checkouts: '+n+'/100. '+(s&&o?'Recommendations omitted.':s?'Optional branch blocks all in this toy.':'Full experience.')+'

';}recLatency.onchange=degradePaint;fallbackMode.onchange=degradePaint;degradePaint();
questions: Payment can be healthy while end-to-end checkout fails.

steps.note: Optional latency blocks the toy path.

steps.code:
fallback_tested=True
served_with_fallback=requests if fallback_tested else served_without_fallback

walkthrough.limit: Executed a Python decision model, not a capacity forecast.

sources: Google SRE: production service best practices
visual_explanation: The architecture separates critical and optional branches; controls change only the optional branch and survival behavior.
written_questions: Which platform dependency is optional during an incident?
What test proves degradation is safe?

title: A tool call is a proposal: validate before the handler
goal: Reject malformed agent arguments before any side effect.
concept:
An agent filling a change form is like a person filling a bank form: plausible text is not an approved instruction. The tool boundary must check structure before the handler runs.

MCP tools advertise an inputSchema. Validation can enforce required fields, types, bounds, and unexpected properties. Authorization and producer approval remain separate gates.
example:
A data-quality tool accepts {dataset, rule_type, threshold}. The agent adds approve:true. A permissive schema lets it reach business code; additionalProperties:false rejects it before registration.

“Valid JSON” is not the same as valid tool input.

use_case.when: Use this for tools that register rules, deploy code, spend money, or change production state.
use_case.example: Validate a proposed data-quality rule before invoking the existing authenticated API.
use_case.decision: Schema covers shape and bounds. Still enforce identity, dataset entitlement, tier approval, idempotency, audit, and semantic rules in the trusted service.

practice: Toggle strictness and proposal shape. Predict handler reachability.
boundary: The browser performs three hand-coded checks, not JSON Schema or MCP. It does not authenticate, authorize, approve, or call an API.
js:
function toolPaint(){const s=schemaMode.value==='strict',k=agentArgs.value,m=k==='missing',x=k==='extra',v=!m&&!(s&&x);world.innerHTML='
1. dataset → '+(m?'MISSING':'PRESENT')+'
2. approve field → '+(x?(s?'REJECTED':'ALLOWED BY SHAPE'):'NONE')+'
3. handler → '+(v?'REACHED; authorization still required':'NOT CALLED')+'
';}schemaMode.onchange=toolPaint;agentArgs.onchange=toolPaint;toolPaint();
questions: It closes the object shape only.
Valid shape can still be unauthorized.

steps.note: Define closed shape and extra proposal.

steps.code:
missing=[k for k in schema["required"] if k not in proposal]
extra=[k for k in proposal if k not in schema["required"]]
handler_called=not missing and (schema["allow_extra"] or not extra)

walkthrough.limit: Executed a Python shape check, not conforming JSON Schema or MCP.

visual_explanation: The visual separates required-field validation, extra-field validation, and the later authorization boundary.
written_questions: Which bounds belong in your DQ tool schema?
Which tier approval stays outside model control?

title: One telescope, two science programs: commensal signal capture
goal: Explain how a sidecar digital backend reuses observations without taking telescope time.
tag: New research review · claims bounded to authors’ report
concept:
A passenger can photograph the view while a train follows its normal route. A commensal astronomy backend receives a copy of telescope signals while the primary program continues.

The advance is architectural and operational—not a claim of detected extraterrestrial life: packetized backends, commodity GPUs, pipelines, archives, and verification workflows let another search piggyback at scale.
example:
The October 5, 2026 Breakthrough Listen decade review describes commensal systems including COSMIC at the VLA and BLUSE at MeerKAT. It reports more than 1.2 million BLUSE pointings since mid-2022 and about 42 PB storage capacity, 31 PB in use, by March 2026.

Our synthetic 4 Gb/s tap for one hour receives 1.8 TB before reduction. Retaining 2% keeps 36 GB. These are teaching inputs, not named-instrument performance.

use_case.when: Relevant to specialist observatories and to architects designing sidecar analytics that must not disturb a primary workload.
use_case.example: Mirror a read-only signal stream to a GPU pipeline while the primary telescope schedule remains authoritative.
use_case.decision: Use only with explicit isolation, bandwidth, backpressure, provenance, and archive budgets. A side tap can harm primary work if shared paths saturate.

practice: Change tap rate and retention. Predict raw and retained volume while observing time stays fixed.
boundary: This is unit conversion, not telescope sensitivity, spectra, compression quality, candidate verification, packet loss, or detection evidence.
js:
function radioPaint(){const r=Number(tapRate.value),p=Number(retainPct.value),raw=r*3600/8/1000,kept=raw*p/100;world.innerHTML='

1 hour raw: '+raw.toFixed(1)+' TB. Retained: '+kept.toFixed(3)+' TB ('+p+'%).

Additional primary observing time in this model: 0 hours.

';}tapRate.onchange=radioPaint;retainPct.onchange=radioPaint;radioPaint();
questions: The side backend receives a copy.
It is an instrumentation and operations review.

walkthrough.limit: Executed Python conversion with synthetic inputs; no instrument is reproduced.

sources: The First Decade of Breakthrough Listen
Breakthrough Listen public data and archiving
visual_explanation: The stream forks without giving scheduling control to the sidecar; quantity labels separate raw ingress from archive.
written_questions: Which shared resource risks primary work?
What provenance belongs with reduced candidates?

title: A tag can move; a full commit SHA cannot
goal: Pin third-party actions to reviewed immutable code and update explicitly.
concept:
A street address can keep its name while the building changes. A Git tag such as v1 is also movable. A full commit SHA identifies one exact Git object.

GitHub documents full-length SHA pinning as the only immutable action reference. It prevents silent ref movement but does not deliver fixes automatically.
example:
Monday: vendor/action@v1 points to reviewed aaa…. Tuesday: the tag moves to bbb…. Unchanged workflow text runs different code. @aaa… stays on reviewed bytes until a pull request changes it.

- uses: vendor/action@a824008085750b8e136effc585c3cd6082bd575f

use_case.when: Use for third-party actions with write access, secrets, OIDC, artifacts, or deployment authority.
use_case.example: Pin a cloud-login action and use controlled dependency updates for new SHAs.
use_case.decision: Pinning stops ref drift. It does not prove code safe or patch dependencies automatically.

practice: Move the tag and compare it with a full SHA.
boundary: The browser maps toy labels; it does not inspect Git objects, signatures, or action code.
js:
function pinPaint(){const p=actionRef.value==='sha',r=p?'aaa':tagState.value,ok=r==='aaa';world.innerHTML='
Workflow → '+(p?'full SHA aaa…':'tag v1')+'
Resolved → '+r+'… '+(ok?'REVIEWED':'CHANGED WITHOUT WORKFLOW DIFF')+'
Update → '+(p?'explicit SHA change':'tag owner can move ref')+'
';}actionRef.onchange=pinPaint;tagState.onchange=pinPaint;pinPaint();
questions: Can run bbb without workflow diff
It fixes the Git object only.
Patch uptake becomes an explicit path.

walkthrough.limit: Executed a Python name model; it did not access GitHub.

visual_explanation: Two references resolve after a tag move: the tag follows new code while the SHA stays attached to reviewed code.
written_questions: Which deployment actions have highest authority?
How will SHA updates be received and tested?

title: Stop routing before the next RPC: gRPC health Watch
goal: Use the standard health stream so clients avoid NOT_SERVING backends.
concept:
A restaurant host stops seating guests in a closed room. Waiting for each guest to find the locked door creates needless failures.

gRPC defines a health service. A client can open streaming Watch for a named service. After NOT_SERVING, health-aware routing avoids that backend; calls can resume after SERVING.
example:
Inventory has A and B. B loses database access but its process stays alive. It publishes NOT_SERVING. With client health checking, four new calls go to A. Without it, two still reach B and fail in this toy.

Unary Check suits monitoring; streaming Watch avoids every connected client polling constantly.

use_case.when: Use when gRPC clients choose among multiple addresses and service readiness can change while connections remain open.
use_case.example: Inventory remains live but cannot query its database, so it reports NOT_SERVING for that service.
use_case.decision: Health guides routing but does not replace deadlines, retries, load shedding, or accurate readiness. Some policies may disable it; UNIMPLEMENTED disables client health checking per the guide.

practice: Mark B unhealthy and toggle client health. Predict four routes.
boundary: The toy has no network, stream delay, resolver, backoff, channel state, or gRPC library.
js:
function healthPaint(){const d=backendB.value==='down',o=healthClient.value==='on',c=d&&o?['A','A','A','A']:['A','B','A','B'],f=d?c.filter(x=>x==='B').length:0;world.innerHTML='

Next: '+c.join(' → ')+'. Failed: '+f+'/4.

';}backendB.onchange=healthPaint;healthClient.onchange=healthPaint;healthPaint();
questions: Server health must be accurate and policy must use it
Bad health logic still routes badly.

steps.code:
eligible=[n for n,s in backends.items() if s=="SERVING"]
routes=[eligible[i%len(eligible)] for i in range(4)]

walkthrough.limit: Executed a Python eligibility model, not a gRPC channel.

visual_explanation: B remains connected but changes readiness and route eligibility, separating transport reachability from service health.
